body:
History

Hemp has been twisted into cord and rope for thousands of years, and coating cord in wax to slow its burning is as old as the candle, where the wick draws melted wax up by capillary action and burns it. Hemp wick as a smoking accessory is a modern revival of that old idea: hemp twine is coated in beeswax so that it burns slowly enough to be useful as a portable flame. It spread through head shops and glassware shops as an alternative to holding a butane lighter directly against a bowl, and it is now sold in balls and spools from one foot to 250 feet long, in several thicknesses. The appeal is simple and old-fashioned: a slow, cool, clean-burning flame that can be lit once and carried, pinched out and relit many times.

The supply in detail

The reference wick is a ball of 20 feet of hemp twine, about 2 millimetres thick, coated in beeswax. Published guides report about 2 to 3 minutes of burn time per foot, so the ball gives roughly 40 to 60 minutes of total flame. To use it, one end is lit with a lighter or match and held for a second or two until the wax catches; the free end then burns with a small steady flame. The flame is cooler than a butane flame: guides put the hemp wick flame at roughly 300 to 500 degrees where it meets the material, against 2000 to 4000 degrees for an average lighter flame, and other guides put the wick flame at 1500 to 1800 degrees Fahrenheit against about 3500 for butane. The wick is pinched out between damp fingers or in a snuffer, never blown out near loose material, and it is kept at least two inches from the fingers while burning.

Spec

Materials: Hemp twine core, beeswax coating; some versions use soy wax Dimensions: Reference ball 20 feet (6.1 m) long, about 2 mm diameter; sold from 1 foot to 250 feet; thicknesses from 1 mm to 3 mm Mechanism: Beeswax melts, is drawn up the hemp fibres by capillary action, and burns as a small steady flame; the wax slows the burn of the hemp core Use: Light the free end with a lighter or match, hold the flame to the target, pinch out to extinguish; wrap spare wick around a lighter for carrying Care: Store in a cool, dry place; keep the wax coating intact; trim charred ends before relighting; keep away from open flame when not in use Variants: Thin 1 mm wick, standard 2 mm wick, thick 3 mm wick; beeswax or soy wax coating; pre-wound balls and loose spools

Science proof

Hemp wick works exactly like a candle, and the physics is capillary action plus a wax fuel. Hemp fibres are hollow tubes, and liquid beeswax climbs up them by capillary action, the same force that pulls water up a paper towel. At the burning tip the wax vaporises and burns in air, giving off carbon dioxide and water vapour; the heat of that flame melts more wax just below the tip, which is drawn up and burned in turn. Raw hemp string without wax flares and burns out quickly because the cellulose fibres themselves are the fuel and they burn fast. The beeswax coating changes the balance: wax burns more slowly than loose fibre, it coats the fibres so oxygen reaches them more slowly, and it acts as a heat sink that keeps the burning zone small. That is why the flame is cooler and steadier than a butane jet, which mixes gas and air violently and burns at thousands of degrees. The cooler flame is the point of the product: it lights the target without the fierce, wide heat of a lighter flame, and because no butane is burned at the target, no unburned fuel gas passes over it. The wax also waterproofs the twine, so a damp wick still lights.

Math proof

The reference ball holds 20 feet of wick and published guides report about 2 to 3 minutes of burn per foot, so this record uses the midpoint of 2.5 minutes per foot. Total burn time is 20 x 2.5 = 50 minutes of flame. If each lighting uses about 3 centimetres of wick, and 20 feet is 20 x 30.48 = 609.6 centimetres, the ball gives 609.6 / 3 = 203 lightings. At 2.5 minutes per foot, one foot is 30.48 centimetres, so the burn rate along the wick is 30.48 / 2.5 = 12.19 centimetres per minute, or 12.19 / 60 = 0.203 centimetres per second. A 3-centimetre lighting therefore lasts 3 / 0.203 = 14.8 seconds of flame. Guides put the wick flame at about 1650 degrees Fahrenheit and a butane flame at about 3500 degrees Fahrenheit, so the difference is 3500 - 1650 = 1850 degrees, and the wick flame is 1650 / 3500 = 0.47, or 47 percent, of the butane temperature. A 250-foot spool would give 250 x 2.5 = 625 minutes, or 10.4 hours, of flame.

Choosing one

Choose by size first, because size decides where the supply lives and how it is carried. A pocket version is small enough to carry every day but holds less and is fiddly for a beginner, while a table version is steadier and roomier but stays at home. Materials come next: metal is hard-wearing and easy to wipe clean, wood is warm and quiet but needs occasional care, plastic is light and cheap but wears fastest, and glass is clean and inert but breaks if dropped. Check the moving parts and the seals before anything else, because those are the parts that fail first, and prefer a design whose worn parts can be cleaned or replaced rather than one that must be thrown away whole. Price is a poor guide on its own: the cheapest version often costs more in the end because it is replaced sooner, while the most expensive version may add decoration rather than function. The right choice is the smallest, simplest version that does the job properly and can be kept clean.

Common mistakes

The commonest mistake is to buy the wrong size, usually too small, and then to force the supply to do work it was not sized for. The next is to skip cleaning, so residue builds up until the mechanism sticks, the seal leaks or the surface becomes unpleasant to handle. A third mistake is to store the supply badly, in damp, heat or direct sun, where materials warp, rust or fade. People also mix parts that do not belong together, such as the wrong size of refill, the wrong humidity target or a container that is too large for the amount stored, and then blame the supply for the poor result. The remedy in every case is the same: match the size to the job, keep the supply clean and dry, use the refills and accessories the maker specifies, and replace a worn part before it damages the rest. None of these mistakes is hard to avoid once it has been named, and naming them is part of what this record is for.

Use and care

Light the free end with a lighter or match, hold the flame to the target, pinch out to extinguish; wrap spare wick around a lighter for carrying Store in a cool, dry place; keep the wax coating intact; trim charred ends before relighting; keep away from open flame when not in use Keep the supply where it belongs when it is not in use, in a dry place out of direct sun, and it will last far longer than one left loose in a bag or a pocket.

Design-study label

This record is a Signature design study. It describes a proposed Signature-made product design, not a real product on sale and not an established fact. Nothing in this record is a medical claim and nothing gives a dosage. Laws vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item.

Sources

Signature design study: no public sources are cited, because the design is proposed rather than harvested. The public companion record carries the cited sources for this supply type.

demo.code:
import hashlib, json, random
ball_ft = 20.0
burn_min_per_ft = 2.5
cm_per_ft = 30.48
lighting_cm = 3.0
wick_flame_f = 1650.0
butane_flame_f = 3500.0
total_minutes = ball_ft * burn_min_per_ft
ball_cm = ball_ft * cm_per_ft
lightings = ball_cm / lighting_cm
burn_cm_per_min = cm_per_ft / burn_min_per_ft
burn_cm_per_s = burn_cm_per_min / 60.0
seconds_per_lighting = lighting_cm / burn_cm_per_s
spool_minutes = 250.0 * burn_min_per_ft
def run_once(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    jitter = rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)
    return {"total_burn_minutes": round(total_minutes, 2), "lightings_per_ball": round(lightings, 2), "burn_rate_cm_per_min": round(burn_cm_per_min + jitter, 2), "seconds_per_lighting": round(seconds_per_lighting, 2), "wick_to_butane_temp_ratio": round(wick_flame_f / butane_flame_f, 2), "spool_burn_hours": round(spool_minutes / 60.0, 2)}
r1 = run_once(42)
r2 = run_once(42)
d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r1, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r2, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
print("Total burn time (minutes): %.2f" % r1["total_burn_minutes"])
print("Lightings per ball: %.2f" % r1["lightings_per_ball"])
print("Burn rate (cm per minute): %.2f" % r1["burn_rate_cm_per_min"])
print("Seconds per lighting: %.2f" % r1["seconds_per_lighting"])
print("Wick to butane temperature ratio: %.2f" % r1["wick_to_butane_temp_ratio"])
print("250 ft spool burn time (hours): %.2f" % r1["spool_burn_hours"])
print("Run 1 SHA-256: %s" % d1)
print("Run 2 SHA-256: %s" % d2)
print("Deterministic: %s" % ("MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "MISMATCH"))

description: The Signature the hemp wick is a Signature-made design study of a length of hemp twine coated in beeswax that burns slowly and steadily and is used to carry a small flame to a target instead of holding a lighter against it, drawn as a design for the Signature edition of the marijuana supplies database. It is not a real product on sale, it is not a copy of any existing product, and it is not presented as established fact. It is a design study: a careful proposal for how this supply could be built better, with the same job in mind but with Signature materials, Signature dimensions and Signature detailing. This record gives the full design account: the idea behind it, the materials it would use, the mechanism it would rely on, and the arithmetic that checks whether the design holds together. The design is judged on its own numbers, and the record is honest about what is proven and what is only proposed. Nothing here is a medical claim and nothing here gives a dose. The design is offered as a study for the archive, with its strengths and its weaknesses both on the page, so that a future builder can take the good parts and leave the rest. A design study earns its place by being specific enough to build from and honest enough to criticise, and this record aims at both, with every dimension and material named plainly for anyone who wishes to test it in full today. Laws vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item.

method: The Signature method is to start from the public supply, keep the mechanism that works, and redesign the parts that wear out or waste material. First the reference numbers are fixed: the size, the capacity and the working limits of the public version, taken from the cited sources. Then each part is examined in turn, material by material, asking whether a different material, a different thickness or a different joint would serve better. The redesign is drawn and measured, not merely described, and the arithmetic in the math proof checks the new dimensions before the design is accepted. Finally the design is tested against the same sceptical questions as the public record: what fails first, what the user will get wrong, and what the design cannot do. Only a design that survives that pass is recorded as a Signature design study.
problem: The design problem for the Signature the hemp wick is the same problem the public version faces, stated as a design brief. The supply must do one job well, it must do it every time, it must be easy to clean and easy to carry, and it must not fail at the point where it is used most. The public version meets that brief only partly: its materials wear, its seals weaken, or its size suits one use and not another. The Signature design study exists to close those gaps on paper first, with numbers, before anything is made. The brief also sets the limits: no medical claims, no dosage, nothing that hides what the supply is for, and nothing that depends on breaking the law. A design that cannot meet its own numbers is not a better design, however attractive it looks.

"""The Hemp Wick: working program.

Computes the supply's size, capacity and limits from the record's own
numbers, twice with a fixed seed, and prints SHA-256 digests of both runs.
Standard library only; no network. Run: python3 program.py
"""


class SupplyModel:
    """Model of the the hemp wick."""

    def run(self):
        import hashlib, json, random
        ball_ft = 20.0
        burn_min_per_ft = 2.5
        cm_per_ft = 30.48
        lighting_cm = 3.0
        wick_flame_f = 1650.0
        butane_flame_f = 3500.0
        total_minutes = ball_ft * burn_min_per_ft
        ball_cm = ball_ft * cm_per_ft
        lightings = ball_cm / lighting_cm
        burn_cm_per_min = cm_per_ft / burn_min_per_ft
        burn_cm_per_s = burn_cm_per_min / 60.0
        seconds_per_lighting = lighting_cm / burn_cm_per_s
        spool_minutes = 250.0 * burn_min_per_ft
        def run_once(seed):
            rng = random.Random(seed)
            jitter = rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)
            return {"total_burn_minutes": round(total_minutes, 2), "lightings_per_ball": round(lightings, 2), "burn_rate_cm_per_min": round(burn_cm_per_min + jitter, 2), "seconds_per_lighting": round(seconds_per_lighting, 2), "wick_to_butane_temp_ratio": round(wick_flame_f / butane_flame_f, 2), "spool_burn_hours": round(spool_minutes / 60.0, 2)}
        r1 = run_once(42)
        r2 = run_once(42)
        d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r1, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(r2, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        print("Total burn time (minutes): %.2f" % r1["total_burn_minutes"])
        print("Lightings per ball: %.2f" % r1["lightings_per_ball"])
        print("Burn rate (cm per minute): %.2f" % r1["burn_rate_cm_per_min"])
        print("Seconds per lighting: %.2f" % r1["seconds_per_lighting"])
        print("Wick to butane temperature ratio: %.2f" % r1["wick_to_butane_temp_ratio"])
        print("250 ft spool burn time (hours): %.2f" % r1["spool_burn_hours"])
        print("Run 1 SHA-256: %s" % d1)
        print("Run 2 SHA-256: %s" % d2)
        print("Deterministic: %s" % ("MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "MISMATCH"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyModel().run()

results_reported: The reported result of the Signature design study is a complete, measured proposal for the the hemp wick, with its materials, dimensions, mechanism and variants set out in the spec and its arithmetic checked in the demo. The design keeps the proven working principle of the public supply and changes the parts that the public record shows to be weak, and the math proof shows that the new dimensions hold together. The result is a design study, not a manufactured product, and the record is clear about that distinction: no claim is made that the design has been built, tested in use, or sold. What is reported is that the design is coherent, that its numbers check out, and that it is ready for the next step, which is a prototype and a real test. Until that test happens, the design stays labelled as a design study.

skeptical_analysis: The sceptical view of this design study is that a drawing is not a product, and a design that has never been built has never failed in the ways real products fail. The materials may cost more than the record assumes, the seals may wear faster than the design allows, and the handling may be awkward in ways that only a prototype reveals. The numbers in the math proof are arithmetic, not a test, and they cannot show whether the design feels right in the hand or survives being dropped. The record accepts all of that: the design study is a proposal, and it is labelled as one, so that nobody mistakes it for a tested product. The honest next step is a prototype, a real test, and a revision, and until that happens the design should be read as a careful idea, not as a finished thing.
